text.title: strict-mode-required-fields Core Rules
text.summary: Five testable rules for producing a Pydantic / JSON-Schema model that passes the OpenAI / Azure / Anthropic strict-mode compiler.

rule.statement: For every object schema submitted under `strict: true`, the `required` array must equal the set of keys in `properties`. No property declared on an object may be absent from `required`.
rule.rationale: Strict-mode compiles the schema into a regular grammar; an "optional" key creates branch non-determinism (skip token vs read token). The OpenAI error `400 Invalid schema for response_format ... required list does not match properties` is the compiler refusing that branch.

rule.statement: Every object schema must set `additionalProperties: false`. Missing or `additionalProperties: true` is a strict-mode rejection.
rule.rationale: Without this, the grammar must accept arbitrary key/value tokens at every object boundary, which collapses the determinism guarantee.

rule.statement: When a field in a strict-mode model encodes absence with a sentinel default — `apartment: str = ""`, `count: int = -1`, `code: str = "N/A"` — the audit MUST report it as a violation and the patch MUST rewrite the field as `T | None = None`, keep it in `required`, and change every downstream consumer that tested `== ""` or `< 0` to test `is None`. The CI step MUST include a round-trip test in which the model emits `null` for that field and the consumer path handles it, and no field in the strict-mode tree keeps a string, negative or zero default that stands for absent. Check that your bridge version translates `T | None` to a nullable-required property (Pydantic 2 with a current openai or anthropic SDK does; older ones may not).

rationale.source: OpenAI Structured Outputs documentation (supported schemas: nullable types); Pydantic documentation (JSON Schema for Optional and Union types); failure mode fm-01 of this methodology

rule.rationale: The sentinel was a workaround for bridges that could not express null, and once the grammar accepts `["string", "null"]` it only hides absence: `""` cannot be told from a deliberately empty value and `-1` is a number the model will happily reason about. Rewriting the consumer at the same time is what makes the change safe — a `None` that reaches code still checking for `""` is a new bug wearing the old one's clothes.

rule.statement: When a field is money or another critical numeric (an amount, a quantity, a score the caller acts on) and it may be absent in the input, the strict-mode model MUST keep the field non-nullable (`total_cents: int`, no `| None`) and MUST pair it with a sibling `refusal: str | None = None` on the same object, in `required`, that the model fills only when it genuinely cannot produce the value. Consumers MUST treat a non-null refusal as a failed extraction and never read the numeric on that row, and the CI walker MUST assert that no money or critical numeric field in the tree carries a nullable type. A nullable amount on this branch is the fm-02 defect.

rationale.source: OpenAI Structured Outputs documentation (refusals); failure mode fm-02 of this methodology

rule.rationale: Making an amount nullable gives the model a legal way to say nothing whenever the extraction is hard, and `null` in a total column is indistinguishable from a real zero-information row by the time it reaches a report. An explicit refusal channel keeps the grammar strict for the number and moves the model's uncertainty into a field that is designed to be read as a failure.

rule.statement: When a field is a free-form metadata bag (`dict[str, Any]`, `extra: dict`, a JSON blob of caller-defined keys), it MUST NOT appear in a schema submitted under `strict: true`, because the bridge emits `additionalProperties: true` for it and the compiler rejects the tree. The audit MUST resolve it one of two ways and record which in the model docstring: when dropping strict mode is acceptable for that call, the call switches to loose JSON mode (`response_format={type: "json_object"}` or `strict: false`) and Pydantic validates the parsed result after the fact; when it is not, the bag is split into a typed sub-object with closed keys and `extra="forbid"` for every key the code reads plus a separate `audit_blob: str` (in `required`, JSON-encoded) for the rest, which consumers `json.loads` and never validate. A `dict[str, Any]` that survives the audit in a strict-mode model is a violation.

rationale.source: OpenAI Structured Outputs documentation (supported schemas: additionalProperties must be false); Pydantic documentation (ConfigDict extra); failure mode fm-05 of this methodology

rule.rationale: Strict mode is a finite grammar and an open dictionary is by definition not finite, so the two cannot share an object; the 400 fires at request time, after review. The split keeps the keys the code actually reads under the grammar and pushes the rest through a string the grammar can bound, which is the only way to have both a closed schema and caller-defined metadata.

rule.statement: Encode "may be absent" by declaring the field as `T | None = None` and keeping it in `required`. Never drop a property from `required` to mean "optional" under strict mode. Empty-string / sentinel encodings are forbidden.
rule.rationale: Strict-mode bridges translate `T | None` into `{"type": ["T", "null"]}` and keep the property required, which is the only encoding the FSM accepts. Sentinels (`""`, `-1`) hide absence and degrade data quality silently.
rule.reference: Reference shape with `notes: str | None = None` encoded as nullable-required.

rule.statement: Set `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` on every Pydantic model whose schema is consumed under strict mode. Apply it to nested models as well — strict mode walks the whole tree.
rule.rationale: `extra="forbid"` is the Pydantic flag that emits `additionalProperties: false` in the JSON Schema. Without it the model defaults to permissive and the schema fails strict-mode submission.

rule.statement: A CI test must call `assert_strict_schema(Model)` (or the equivalent JSON-walker) for every model used in a strict-mode call. The walker asserts on every object node: (a) `additionalProperties is False`, (b) `set(properties.keys()) == set(required)`. CI failure here blocks the merge.
rule.rationale: The strict-mode 400 fires at request time, not build time. Without a CI assertion, the regression escapes review and production rejects the first traffic that uses the new model.
rule.reference: Includes the canonical `assert_strict_schema()` walker; copy verbatim into CI tests.
